common_name: Elsa Sass Peony (Compact Double White Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface. Bred by the Sass brothers of Nebraska and introduced in 1930, Elsa Sass produces fully double, pure white flowers that open from buds carrying a soft blush-pink flush, on a noticeably compact, sturdy plant that rarely needs staking despite the size of its blooms. It flowers in the late midseason window, extending the peony display after many early cultivars have finished, and carries a light, classic peony fragrance. Its shorter stature makes it a good choice for the front of a border or for gardeners who want full, formal double flowers without the floppiness some tall double whites develop after rain. Established clumps are long-lived and rarely need division.
sources: Cricket Hill Garden peony cultivar notes

common_name: Baroness Schroeder Peony (Fragrant Blush-to-White Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced by Kelway & Son of England in 1889, Baroness Schroeder remains one of the most enduringly popular heirloom peonies for its huge, fully double, blush-pink flowers that fade to near-white as they age, giving a single plant a two-tone display over its bloom period. It is considered among the most intensely and sweetly fragrant of all peony cultivars, a trait breeders have used it for repeatedly in later crosses. Bloom comes in the late-midseason window on tall, vigorous, strong stems that generally support the heavy flowers without staking in average garden conditions. Over a century after its introduction it is still widely sold by specialty peony nurseries.

common_name: Philippe Rivoire Peony (Intensely Fragrant Dark Red Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Bred by Riviere and introduced in France in 1911, Philippe Rivoire bears deep garnet-to-maroon double flowers that open nearly black-red in bud before relaxing to a rich wine red, and is widely regarded as one of the most powerfully and richly fragrant of all dark red peonies. Bloom comes in the midseason window on strong, upright stems, though the heavy dark flowers benefit from support in exposed sites or after hard rain. Its saturated color and fragrance have kept it in steady demand from specialty peony growers for more than a century, and it remains a favorite for cutting despite a smaller flower count per plant than some modern reds.

common_name: Solange Peony (Amber-Flushed Cream Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Bred by Lemoine and introduced in 1907, Solange opens creamy white flushed with soft amber and peach tones deep in the flower, an unusual, muted color combination for a peony of its era that has drawn comparisons to old garden roses. The fully double flowers age toward a paler ivory as they mature, and bloom arrives in the late-season window, helping extend the peony display after earlier pinks and whites finish. Strong stems generally hold the flowers upright without staking, and the plant is a reliable, long-lived garden performer once established.

common_name: Walter Faxon Peony (AGM Rose-Pink Heirloom Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Bred by Richardson and introduced in 1904, Walter Faxon carries fully double, clear rose-pink flowers that soften to a paler pink as they age, giving a mature clump a blended range of pink tones at once. It has held a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, a mark of its reliability and garden performance across many decades of cultivation. Bloom falls in the midseason window on sturdy stems, with a light, classic peony fragrance, and the plant is a vigorous, dependable grower that multiplies well once established.

common_name: Laura Dessert Peony (Cream and Yellow-Center Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Bred by Dessert and introduced in France in 1913, Laura Dessert opens creamy white outer guard petals surrounding a dense, canary-yellow bomb-form center that fades toward cream as the flower ages, one of the earliest and most influential yellow-toned lactiflora cultivars and a parent behind many later cream and yellow peonies. Bloom comes early in the peony season on strong stems, with a rich, sweet fragrance. It remains a benchmark cultivar among collectors for its color and form, and specialty peony nurseries still carry it more than a century after its introduction.

common_name: Primevere Peony (Pale Yellow-Centered Bomb-Form Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Bred by Lemoine and introduced in 1907, Primevere carries broad, creamy-white outer guard petals surrounding a full, pale sulfur-yellow bomb-form center that fades to cream as the bloom matures, giving the flower a soft, layered two-tone look. Flowering falls in the midseason window on sturdy stems that hold the large blooms well, with a light fragrance. Along with contemporaries like Laura Dessert, it was one of the early French introductions that helped push lactiflora breeding toward yellow and cream tones, and it remains available through specialty peony growers today.

common_name: Myrtle Gentry Peony (Fragrant Blush-to-White Late Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Introduced by Franklin in 1928, Myrtle Gentry produces large, fully double blush-pink flowers that fade to nearly white as they open fully, carrying a strong, sweet fragrance that ranks it among the most fragrant peonies in commerce. Bloom comes late in the peony season, on tall, strong stems that hold the heavy flowers well without staking in most gardens, extending the display after earlier pinks and whites have finished. It is a vigorous, reliable grower long favored by cut-flower growers for its scent and stem strength.

common_name: Henry Bockstoce Peony (Late-Blooming Dark Red Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Introduced by Bockstoce in 1955, Henry Bockstoce bears large, fully double, dark red flowers on tall, strong stems, and is valued in cut-flower and show circles as one of the latest-blooming red peonies, opening well after most other reds have finished. Its late timing lets gardeners extend the red peony display into the tail end of the season, and its sturdy stems generally support the heavy blooms without staking. Established clumps are vigorous and floriferous, producing abundant cut flowers each spring once mature.

common_name: James Kelway Peony (Early Fragrant White Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Introduced by Kelway & Son in 1900, James Kelway bears large, fully double white flowers with faint creamy-blush flecks at the base of the inner petals, opening early in the peony season on tall, vigorous stems. It carries a strong, sweet fragrance and has remained in commerce for well over a century thanks to its reliable vigor and clean white color. As an early bloomer it pairs well in a border with later pink and red cultivars to extend the overall peony display.

common_name: Frances Willard Peony (Blush-Flecked White Double Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Introduced by Brand in 1932, Frances Willard opens pale blush pink and matures to white, with faint crimson flecks scattered near the center of the fully double flower, a signature trait of many Brand-bred peonies. Bloom comes in the midseason window on strong stems, with a light, sweet fragrance. It has stayed in specialty commerce for close to a century on the strength of its clean color, dependable bloom, and vigorous, long-lived growth habit.

common_name: Martha Bulloch Peony (Large-Flowered Rose-Pink Bomb Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Introduced by Brand in 1907, Martha Bulloch bears enormous, fully double, rose-pink bomb-form flowers that rank among the largest blooms of any lactiflora cultivar, with a strong, sweet fragrance. Bloom falls in the midseason to late-midseason window on sturdy stems, though the sheer size and weight of the flowers benefit from support after heavy rain. It has been prized by exhibitors and collectors for more than a century for its flower size, and mature clumps make an imposing specimen in a perennial border.

common_name: Auguste Dessert Peony (Silver-Tipped Rose-Pink Crown Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Introduced by Dessert in France in 1920, Auguste Dessert carries rose-pink outer guard petals with a distinctive silvery reverse, surrounding a crown-form center of cream petals flecked with crimson, a striking bicolor combination for a lactiflora of its era. Bloom comes in the midseason window on reliable stems, with a light fragrance. Its unusual color pattern has kept it popular among collectors of heirloom French peony cultivars, and it remains obtainable from specialty peony nurseries.

common_name: Inspecteur Lavergne Peony (Bright Red Double Cut-Flower Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, setting the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Introduced by Dessert in France in 1924, Inspecteur Lavergne produces bright, clear red, fully double flowers on upright stems, opening in the midseason window with a light fragrance. Its saturated, true-red color and reliable stem strength have made it a long-standing favorite for cutting, and it continues to be offered by specialty peony growers a century after its introduction. Established plants bloom heavily and are easy to grow in average garden soil.

common_name: Callie's Memory Itoh Peony (Yellow Intersectional Peony with Red Flares)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Callie's Memory is an Anderson-bred intersectional (Itoh) hybrid producing large, semi-double to nearly single soft yellow flowers marked with bold raspberry-red flares radiating from the center of each petal, opening a few days ahead of the well-known yellow Itoh 'Bartzella'. Like other Itoh hybrids it carries strong, woody-based stems that hold the flowers upright without staking, glossy deeply-cut foliage that stays attractive through summer, and better tolerance of heat and a wider soil pH range than straight herbaceous peonies. It dies back to the ground each winter rather than persisting as a woody shrub, and its strong fragrance makes it a favorite for cutting.

common_name: Border Charm Itoh Peony (Butter-Yellow Intersectional Peony with Golden Spring Foliage)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Border Charm is an Anderson-bred Itoh hybrid noted for its pale, butter-yellow, semi-double flowers marked with small maroon flares at the base of each petal, and for foliage that emerges with a distinct yellow-gold tint in spring before settling to green, a trait that makes the clump ornamental even before bloom. Strong, self-supporting stems and glossy, deeply-cut leaves keep the plant attractive through the growing season, and like other Itoh hybrids it tolerates more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight herbaceous peonies while dying back to the ground each winter.

common_name: Morning Lilac Itoh Peony (Lavender-Pink Intersectional Peony)

directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with the eyes no more than 1-2 inches below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Morning Lilac is an Itoh hybrid bearing semi-double, lavender-pink flowers with a deeper rose-purple flare toward the center, a color range that sets it apart from the yellow and cream tones common among many Itoh cultivars. Strong, woody-based stems hold the blooms upright without staking, and the deeply cut, glossy foliage remains attractive well after flowering into fall. As with other Itoh hybrids it tolerates more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight herbaceous lactiflora cultivars, while dying back to the ground each winter rather than persisting as a woody shrub.

common_name: Hana Kisoi Tree Peony (Ruffled Deep Rose-Pink Japanese Tree Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting a grafted union 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Hana Kisoi is a widely grown Japanese tree peony cultivar bearing huge, semi-double flowers with ruffled, crepe-textured petals surrounding bright golden stamens, opening in mid-to-late spring roughly a week or two ahead of most herbaceous peonies. It is a vigorous, floriferous grower that has become one of the more commonly available Japanese tree peony cultivars in the American nursery trade. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture where summers turn hot and humid, and avoid heavy pruning, since flower buds form on the prior year's wood; remove only dead or damaged growth.
sources: Cricket Hill Garden tree peony cultivar notes

common_name: Shima Nishiki Tree Peony (Red-and-White Striped Japanese Tree Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting a grafted union 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Shima Nishiki ('striped brocade') is a Japanese tree peony sport of the red cultivar 'Taiyo' and is best known for its genetically unstable, semi-double flowers streaked and splashed with red and white in irregular patterns on the same bloom; individual flowers, and even whole branches, can occasionally revert to solid red or solid white, so no two seasons look quite the same. Opening in mid-to-late spring on the same vigorous framework typical of suffruticosa cultivars, it is prized by collectors specifically for this unpredictable variegation. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

common_name: Godaishu Tree Peony (Vigorous White Japanese Tree Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting a grafted union 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Godaishu (a name often translated as 'five continents') is a Japanese tree peony cultivar bearing large, semi-double to double, pure white flowers with prominent golden stamens, opening in mid-to-late spring on one of the more vigorous, quick-to-establish growth habits among white-flowered suffruticosa cultivars. Its clean white color and reliable performance have made it a popular choice among Western tree peony growers looking for a dependable white selection. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

common_name: Renkaku Tree Peony (Flight of Cranes White Japanese Tree Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting a grafted union 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Renkaku ('flight of cranes') is one of the most widely planted white Japanese tree peony cultivars in Western gardens, bearing large, semi-double, pure white flowers with softly ruffled, crepe-textured petals and bright yellow stamens, opening in mid-to-late spring on a vigorous, well-branched framework. Its dependable bloom and strong growth have made it a benchmark white selection recommended by tree peony specialists for gardeners new to the group. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

common_name: Taiyo Tree Peony (Vivid Red Japanese Tree Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting a grafted union 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Taiyo ('the sun') is a Japanese tree peony cultivar bearing large, semi-double flowers in a vivid, glowing red-orange, one of the brightest reds among commonly available suffruticosa selections, opening in mid-to-late spring on a vigorous, upright framework. It is also notable as the parent from which the red-and-white streaked sport 'Shima Nishiki' arose, and unlike its unstable offspring, Taiyo itself blooms a consistent, saturated red each year. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

common_name: Black Pirate Tree Peony (Near-Black Daphnis Hybrid Tree Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting a grafted union 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Black Pirate is an American tree peony hybrid bred by Nassos Daphnis, part of a line of hybrids he developed crossing Paeonia suffruticosa with P. delavayi and P. potaninii to push tree peony color toward deep, near-black reds not found in the traditional Japanese and Chinese cultivar groups. Its semi-double flowers open a deep maroon-black that reads almost black in low light, set against glossy, dark-tinted foliage, opening in mid-to-late spring on a somewhat more compact, twiggy framework than many Japanese suffruticosa selections. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.
sources: Cricket Hill Garden tree peony cultivar notes
